text: TrafficFlowBench, the twenty twenty-six IEEE BigData Cup. Eight hundred and two teams. We finished eighth on the private leaderboard. This is how.

The data is a synthetic freeway network: ten directional corridors, one reading every five minutes. Four tasks share one score. Fill in hidden speed and flow. Forecast where queues start, and where they persist. Keep the traffic physics consistent. And estimate origin to destination demand. March is the public board. April is the private one. And the organisers generated the two months independently, with different incidents.

That last fact shaped everything. Each month is its own scenario. Gains learned on the training months reached the board at a fifth of their size, or flipped sign. Gains learned on the scored month itself landed where we forecast them: a median of one point zero times the prediction. So the rule became simple. Learn on the month you are scored on.

Here is the final system. Each scored month is built on its own. For state, a LightGBM stack feeds a masked U-Net, trained per corridor on that month's own released cells, then refined. Physics has no model of its own; it scores our state. The two queue tasks use online models that see only data stamped before the forecast time, fine-tuned date by date. And for demand, the organisers' own least-squares solver: every move away from it lost.

text: The largest late gains came from new label sources, not new inputs. Released cells of the scored month, hidden from the model and used as training targets, paid three times in a row. On a held-out March day, the error at those hidden cells is two kilometres per hour, against a spread of nineteen.

None of this works without honest measurement. Ninety of our ninety-one submissions carried a forecast written before the upload. State changes landed on the line. Queue changes scattered, so we built an instrument for each component and gated it before use. Every idea went into a registry: two hundred and sixty-seven ideas, forty-five adopted, one hundred and eight refuted, each with the smallest effect its test could see.

Step by step, the public score climbed from point eight three seven, to point nine zero zero eight eight. On the private board, April, our final file scored point eight nine eight seven four. Eighth of eight hundred and two.

Everything is open. One script rebuilds the scored submission from the competition data and our released weights. In a clean folder, made only from the public repository, the rebuilt file is byte for byte identical to the one we submitted.
